desc:
Swift package and SDK development turns code you keep repeating into a reusable, tested library. Ecom Swift LLC builds clean Swift packages for Swift Package Manager, with unit tests, documentation and versioning, so your apps and your team can share one source of truth.

## What is a Swift package?

A Swift package is a folder of Swift code with a manifest file that tells Xcode how to build it. You add it to an app by pointing to its location, and Swift Package Manager downloads and builds it. A package can hold networking code, UI components, data models, analytics wrappers or a complete SDK for a service.

An SDK, or software development kit, is a package designed for other developers to use. Its public interface is small and documented, and it hides the details behind it.

## Why shared code belongs in a package

When several apps copy the same code, each copy slowly changes. A bug fixed in one is still present in the others, and a new developer has no idea which version is correct. Updates become tedious, and mistakes multiply.

A package gives that code one home. You fix an issue once, tag a new version and update each app deliberately. Tests in the package catch regressions before they reach users, and the README shows a new developer how to use it in minutes.

## How a good package affects your team

The benefit is time and quality. Features reach each app faster because the building blocks already exist. Behavior stays consistent across products, which matters for sign-in, payments and branding.

For companies that offer a service to other developers, an SDK is part of the product. A clear, stable interface makes your service easier to adopt, and good documentation reduces support questions.

## What a well-made Swift package includes

- A small public interface, with internal details kept private.
- Clear names and types that read well at the call site.
- Unit tests for the main functions and edge cases.
- A README with installation steps and short, working examples.
- DocC documentation for the public interface, in larger packages.
- Semantic version tags, so apps can update safely.
- A manifest that supports the iOS and macOS versions you need.
- An example app that shows real usage, in the Standard package.
- Continuous integration that builds and tests on every change, in Premium.

## How we build it

We begin by asking what the package must do and who will use it. If the code already exists inside an app, we study it and decide what belongs in the package and what stays in the app. Then we design the public interface first, write the tests, and build the implementation behind it.

The Basic package delivers one focused package with tests and a README. Standard covers up to three related modules, DocC documentation, an example app and version tags. Premium builds a full SDK with a networking and error handling layer, release setup, a migration guide and a walkthrough call.

You can keep the package in a private repository for your team, or publish it yourself.

## Extracting code from an existing app

Pulling code out of a live app is a delicate step. Hidden dependencies, shared global state and tangled view code can make a clean split harder than expected. We separate the logic first, add tests around it, then move it and replace the old code in your app with calls into the package. This keeps the app working at every stage.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- List the apps or teams that will use the package.
- Expose only the types and functions that users really need.
- Use semantic versions and write release notes.
- Add tests before changing a package that others depend on.
- Document breaking changes in a migration guide.

**Avoid:**
- Exposing internal types that you may want to change later.
- Making the package depend on a particular app.
- Bundling unrelated features into one module.
- Releasing changes without a new version tag.
- Skipping the README because the code seems obvious.

## Who this is for

A team that maintains several apps and keeps copying code between them is the typical buyer. A company that offers an API and wants a Swift client for its customers also fits, as does a developer who wants to clean up a growing project into separate modules.

## What we need from you

Tell us what the package should do and which code, if any, it should come from. Share the repository as a collaborator invitation, and any API documentation for the service involved. You decide where the package lives and who owns it, and the source code is yours. We never need your passwords.
